paragraphs: One who did not sleep on the night of Erev Rosh Hashanah may eat until dawn (amud ha-shachar), but one who slept should not eat after sleeping, and only a drink of coffee is permitted before dawn (alot ha-shachar).

clarification.explanation: One who did not sleep on the night of Erev Rosh Hashanah may eat until dawn. But one who has already slept should not eat after sleeping, and only drinking coffee is permitted to him before dawn.
takeaways: One who did not sleep: may eat until dawn
One who slept: may not eat after sleeping, and only coffee is permitted

paragraphs: One does not blow the shofar on Erev Rosh Hashanah, neither by day nor by night, even in one's home. If the community's shofar-blower wants to practice and needs to do so, he should blow it in a closed room or in a pit. One does not fall on one's face (Tachanun) on Erev Rosh Hashanah, but at the Minchah before it one does fall and recite Vidui (confession), since on the night of Erev Rosh Hashanah Vidui and Selichot are recited, and it is customary to go to the cemetery on Erev Rosh Hashanah and recite supplications there. One should not direct his intent toward the dead, but rather pray to Hashem, may He be blessed, that He grant him mercy in their merit; and one may prostrate himself on the grave of a righteous person and say: "I hereby ask of the soul of the righteous one buried here that he pray for me before the Holy One, blessed be He, for such-and-such." And one should be careful with the Minchah prayer of Erev Rosh Hashanah, since it is the last prayer (of that year).

clarification.explanation: One does not blow the shofar on Erev Rosh Hashanah, neither by day nor by night, even at home; and the community's shofar-blower who needs to practice should do so in a closed room or in a pit. One does not recite Tachanun (falling on one's face) on Erev Rosh Hashanah itself, but at the Minchah of Erev Rosh Hashanah one does fall and recite Vidui, and likewise Vidui and Selichot are recited on the night of Erev Rosh Hashanah. It is customary to go to the cemetery on Erev Rosh Hashanah and recite supplications there; but one should not direct his intent to the dead themselves, rather pray to Hashem that He grant mercy in their merit, and one may ask the soul of a righteous person to pray for him before Hashem. One should be especially careful with the Minchah prayer of Erev Rosh Hashanah, since it is the last prayer of the year.
takeaways: The shofar is not blown on Erev Rosh Hashanah, and Tachanun is not recited during the day, but it is recited at the Minchah before it
At the cemetery one prays to Hashem in the merit of the righteous, not to the dead themselves

paragraphs: One takes a haircut on Erev Rosh Hashanah, and it is good to be careful to do so before midday; and while cutting his hair, one should intend to remove the forces of judgment and to fulfill the mitzvah of pe'ot (sidelocks). One wears white clothing on Rosh Hashanah out of our faith and trust in the kindnesses of Hashem, may He be blessed - this is based on what our Sages expounded in the Midrash, as cited in the Levush. It is customary to immerse on Erev Rosh Hashanah, because of possible seminal emission - since a drop might emerge from him through some change without his awareness - and also because of the impurity of marital relations, and also in order to receive the illumination of the holiness of the Yom Tov of Rosh Hashanah for a good life and peace. Therefore, in the first immersion he should intend for purity; in the second, for the rectification of anger; in the third, to sweeten judgment and severity with kindness; in the fourth, to remove from himself the garments of the weekday, intending also "let the year and its curses end"; and in the fifth, to receive upon himself the illumination of the holiness of the Day of Remembrance, intending "let the year and its blessings begin." Women, too, should be careful to immerse on Erev Rosh Hashanah, even unmarried maidens, and they must first comb the hair of their head because of interposition (chatzitzah), and likewise check their bodies for other interposing matters; only they need not remove the hair of the armpits and the pubic area - see Matteh Efraim.

If a man is prevented by circumstance from immersing, he should pour nine kabbin of water (approximately twelve and six-tenths liters) over his body while standing naked, and another person should come and pour the water over him from his head to his feet. These nine kabbin - each kav is 432 dirhams, for each kav is four log and each log is 108 dirhams, as mentioned in Beit David, page 136. And if he does not have one vessel that can hold all nine kabbin, he should divide them between two or three vessels, but more than three vessels may not be combined; and he must be careful to pour the second before the first stream ends, and likewise for the third - as mentioned in the Mishnah, Chapter 3 of Mikvaot; see the Shulchan Aruch of the Gaon Rabbeinu Zalman, siman 606, and what is written in the Turei Zahav, siman 88, is a scribal error. And if even this he cannot do, it is good that he wash his hands forty times, in this order: he should first pour once on his right hand, intending the first letter of the Name of seventy-two [letters]; likewise once on his left hand, also intending the first letter of the Name of seventy-two; then he should pour a second time on the right, intending the second letter of the Name of seventy-two, and likewise a second time on the left, intending the second letter, and so on in this manner ten times; and he should then repeat and pour ten times in succession on the right, intending each time one letter of the ten letters of the Name of seventy-two, and afterward pour ten times in succession on the left, intending in them the ten letters of the Name of seventy-two in order - the total sum being forty times, as mentioned in the book Emet LeYaakov by his grandsons, in the pamphlet Sefat Emet; see there.

clarification.explanation: One takes a haircut on Erev Rosh Hashanah, and it is good to take it before midday, intending to remove the forces of judgment and to fulfill the mitzvah of pe'ot. One wears white clothing on Rosh Hashanah out of faith and trust in the kindnesses of Hashem. It is customary to immerse on Erev Rosh Hashanah, out of concern for a drop of seminal emission, because of the impurity of marital relations, and in order to receive the holiness of the day; and one intends in the immersions: purity, rectifying anger, sweetening judgment, removing the weekday garments ("let the year and its curses end"), and receiving the holiness of the Day of Remembrance ("let the year and its blessings begin"). Women too, even unmarried maidens, should immerse, and should comb their hair and check their bodies for interposing matter (though there is no need to remove the hair of the armpits and pubic area). One who is prevented from immersing should pour nine kabbin of water (about 12.6 liters) over his body while standing naked, and another person should pour it over him from head to foot; it may be divided between two or three vessels (no more), provided the second is poured before the first stream ends. And if even this cannot be done, it is good to wash the hands forty times alternately (right and left), with the intentions of the letters of the Name of seventy-two.
takeaways: One takes a haircut, wears white, and immerses on Erev Rosh Hashanah (women and unmarried maidens as well)
One who cannot immerse: nine kabbin of water, or, if pressed, washing the hands forty times

paragraphs: One should be accustomed to eat on Rosh Hashanah, on both nights, at his table in this order: first dates, and he blesses "Borei Peri Ha'etz" and eats one date, and afterward says "May it be Your will that our enemies be finished," etc., and eats the second date, intending in this request regarding the "lower" enemies. Afterward he eats rubia - which in Arabic is called lubia - and says "May it be Your will that our merits increase." And according to what the Gaon Magen Avraham wrote, that one should also make the request according to the meaning apparent from the language of the country, therefore we, the people of Baghdad, who call it lubia, must say "that his merits increase and win our hearts." As we are accustomed to say, in the Keriah [tearing], two requests: "that You tear the harshness of our verdict" and "let our merits be read before You" - which is the meaning of tearing, based on the word kera - so is the matter with rubia, according to the language of our country. After the rubia he eats karti (leek) and says "that our enemies and haters be cut off," intending this regarding the evil forces created from a person's sins and from sparks of seminal emission, concerning which we have intent in the Shema recited upon the bed, and of which it is said, "a man's enemies are the men of his own house." After the karti he eats silka (beet) and says "that our enemies be removed," etc., intending this regarding the prosecutors and the forces of judgment that accuse above. Afterward he eats kara (gourd) and says "that You tear the harshness of our verdict" (intending the word kera) "and let our merits be read before You." Afterward he eats a sweet pomegranate and says "that we be filled with merits like a pomegranate." Afterward he eats an apple cooked in sugar and says "May it be Your will that a good and sweet year be renewed upon us" - and one does not say "like honey." The later authorities wrote the reason that an apple is brought as an allusion to the "holy field of apples" (chakal tapuchin kadishin), based on the secret of "See, the scent of my son is like the scent of the field." And it appears to me, with the help of Heaven, another reason for the apple on the night of Rosh Hashanah: the apple has three pleasures - taste, appearance, and smell - and this is a good sign for our request for general abundance, which is "children, life, and sustenance," for the whole year. And it further appears to me, with the help of Heaven, another reason, based on what is written in the Holy Zohar, Parashat Shemini, page 40, on the verse "Sustain me with apples": the apple counters wine, meaning it prevents the wine from causing harm - and so one eats an apple after wine so that the wine will not harm him, and therefore it is the custom of people to put an apple into the cup of wine, as is written in the books. And it is known that wine represents the forces of severity (gevurot), so the apple sweetens the severities; and now, on Rosh Hashanah, our whole intent is to sweeten and soften the severities, and therefore we eat an apple. And it further appears to me, with the help of Heaven, another reason: it is stated in the Holy Zohar that all fruits are rooted in Malchut, and only the apple is rooted in the male aspect (duchra), which is the secret of Tiferet, as I have written this introduction elsewhere; and it is known what our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, wrote, that the summer months are in the female aspect (nukva), which is the secret of Malchut, from Nissan to Tishrei, and the winter months from Tishrei to Nissan are in the male aspect, which is the secret of Tiferet; therefore on the night of Rosh Hashanah, which is the beginning of the male-aspect months, we eat an apple, whose root is in the male aspect.

After the apple it is customary to eat the head of a sheep, requesting "May it be Your will that we be as a head and not as a tail" and "remember for us the binding (Akedah) of Isaac our father, the son of Abraham our father, peace be upon them." And if one could not bring the head of a sheep, one should not bring the head of a goat instead, because it alludes to "harsh judgment," as mentioned in the Holy Zohar, Parashat Shemini, page 41, side 2, and see further in the Zohar Chadash, Seder Toldot. Therefore it is good that a person not raise a goat in his home, or at least be careful about this on Rosh Hashanah and the rest of the Ten Days of Repentance, that he not find a goat in his house; and therefore he should not bring before him on Rosh Hashanah the head of a goat - and if he cannot find the head of a sheep, he should bring the head of a fowl instead. It must be brought cooked, and therefore he should pierce the skull, salt it, and cook it; and the head of a male fowl is better than that of a female fowl, as a good omen. And when he brings the head of a fowl, he should say only the request "that we be as a head and not as a tail," but one does not say "and remember for us the binding of Isaac our father" except with the head of a sheep. Some make the order mentioned above with the foods mentioned above also on the day of Rosh Hashanah, at Shacharit, as mentioned in Matteh Efraim; and so we are accustomed in our home, to bring all that was mentioned above to the table also during the day.

clarification.explanation: One should be accustomed to hold, on both nights of Rosh Hashanah, an order of omen-foods (simanim) at his table: first dates, with the blessing "Borei Peri Ha'etz" and eating a date, then saying "May it be Your will that our enemies be finished" and eating a second date. Then rubia (lubia), saying "that our merits increase and win our hearts"; karti (leek), "that our enemies be cut off"; silka (beet), "that our enemies be removed" (regarding the accusers); kara (gourd), "that the harshness of our verdict be torn and our merits be read before You"; a sweet pomegranate, "that we be filled with mitzvot like a pomegranate"; and an apple cooked in sugar, "that a good and sweet year be renewed upon us" (and one does not say "like honey"). The later authorities wrote that eating the apple alludes to the "holy field of apples" - a holy field mentioned in the secret of the Zohar - based on the verse "See, the scent of my son is like the scent of the field." And our teacher [the Ben Ish Chai] added further reasons of his own for eating the apple, among them: that it has three pleasures (taste, appearance, and smell) as a sign of general abundance of children, life, and sustenance; that the apple sweetens the severities (as an apple is placed in wine); and that its root is in the aspect of "the male" (Tiferet), with which the winter months begin. After the apple, one eats the head of a sheep - bringing it cooked: piercing the skull, salting, and cooking it - and requests "that we be as a head and not as a tail" and "remember for us the binding of Isaac." One should not bring the head of a goat, which represents harsh judgment (and it is good not to raise a goat at home, especially during the Ten Days of Repentance); and if there is no head of a sheep, one brings the head of a fowl (male preferred), saying regarding it only "that we be as a head and not as a tail." Some hold this order also on the day of Rosh Hashanah at Shacharit, and so did [the Ben Ish Chai] practice.
takeaways: The order of omen-foods on both nights: date, rubia, karti, silka, kara, pomegranate, apple, sheep's head

The apple is eaten for several reasons: a kabbalistic allusion to the "holy field of apples" in the Zohar, its three pleasures (taste, appearance, and smell), the sweetening of the severities, and its root in the attribute of Tiferet
One does not bring the head of a goat (harsh judgment); in the absence of a sheep's head one brings the head of a fowl

paragraphs: One should not eat on Rosh Hashanah anything sour, nor a dish cooked with something sour, and one should likewise be careful of sour fruits - be they pomegranates, grapes, or pears - and Matteh Efraim wrote that the same law applies to a fruit that has not yet fully ripened. It is a good custom to eat fatty meat and sweet foods as a good omen, but one should not indulge in them to fill his stomach, rather "[only] its tasters merit life." And one should drink pleasant drinks, based on what is written in Ezra: "Eat the fat and drink the sweet, and send portions to him who has nothing prepared, for this day is holy to our Lord; and do not be sad, for the joy of Hashem is your strength" - for this verse is said regarding the day of Rosh Hashanah, as is known.

clarification.explanation: One does not eat anything sour on Rosh Hashanah, nor a dish cooked with something sour, and one should be careful of sour fruits (pomegranates, grapes, sour pears), and likewise of a fruit that has not finished ripening. It is a good custom to eat fatty meat and sweet foods as a good omen, but one should not indulge to the point of filling his stomach, for "its tasters merit life"; and one should drink pleasant drinks, based on the verse in Ezra, "Eat the fat and drink the sweet... for the joy of Hashem is your strength," which is said regarding Rosh Hashanah.
takeaways: One does not eat sour food, sour fruits, or fruit that has not finished ripening
One eats fatty meat and sweets as a good omen, but in moderation, not to excess

paragraphs: One should be careful not to become angry, for beyond the gravity of the prohibition against anger, which is severe at all times, on the day of Rosh Hashanah it is not a good omen for a person. And the wife should be diligent to set the table and cover it with a fine cloth before her husband comes from the synagogue, so that when he arrives he will find the table set - a good omen. If it happens that he comes and does not find the table set, he should not quarrel with his wife or become angry, for anger is an especially bad omen; rather he should bear it and not be resentful even in his heart.

clarification.explanation: One should be careful not to become angry, for besides the gravity of the prohibition of anger at all times, on Rosh Hashanah it is not a good omen. The wife should be diligent to set the table and cover it with a fine cloth before her husband comes from the synagogue, so the table will be found set - a good omen. And if it happens that he comes and does not find the table set, he should not quarrel with his wife or become angry, for anger is an especially bad omen; rather he should bear it and not be resentful even in his heart.
takeaways: Care about not becoming angry is especially great on Rosh Hashanah, since it is not a good omen
The wife sets the table before the husband's arrival, and the husband should not be resentful even in his heart

paragraphs: Before Kiddush he should sit in his place on a made bed and recite the "Petichat Eliyahu" [Opening of Elijah], of blessed memory, until "Kum Rabbi Shimon veyitchadshun" [Arise, Rabbi Shimon, and let them be renewed], etc. Afterward he should say the verse (Genesis 6:8) "And Noah found favor in the eyes of Hashem" twelve times, and afterward the verse (ibid. 26:12) "And Isaac sowed in that land," etc., twelve times, and afterward the verse (Psalms 36:10) "For with You is the fountain of life; in Your light do we see light," ten times, and afterward the verse (ibid. 97:11) "Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright of heart," seventeen times, and afterward (I Samuel 25:6) "And you shall say, So, may you live, and peace be to you, and peace to your house," etc., ten times, and he should say "Techel shanah u'birchoteha" [Let the year and its blessings begin] and stand to recite Kiddush.

clarification.explanation: Before Kiddush he sits on a made bed and recites "Petichat Eliyahu" until "Kum Rabbi Shimon." Afterward he says the verse "And Noah found favor in the eyes of Hashem" twelve times, "And Isaac sowed in that land" twelve times, "For with You is the fountain of life; in Your light do we see light" ten times, "Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright of heart" seventeen times, and "So may you live, and peace be to you, and peace to your house" ten times, and says "Let the year and its blessings begin" and stands to recite Kiddush.
takeaways: Before Kiddush one recites "Petichat Eliyahu" and verses a set number of times
One concludes with "Let the year and its blessings begin" and stands to recite Kiddush

paragraphs: At the Kiddush on both nights he blesses "Shehecheyanu," and if he happens to have a new fruit, he should place it before him on the table on the second night when he blesses "Shehecheyanu" and intend upon it, but there is no need to insist on repeating this matter. And he should do the entire order of the first night on the second night as well, and he should study at the table on both nights a Mishnah from Tractate Rosh Hashanah, intending [the study] toward the Name Adonai; but he should be careful to study it with a pleasant melody, and it is customary to study also the language of the Holy Zohar printed in the Machzorim.

clarification.explanation: At the Kiddush of both nights, one blesses "Shehecheyanu." If he has a new fruit, he should place it before him on the second night at the time of the "Shehecheyanu" blessing and intend upon it, though there is no need to insist on this. The whole order of the first night is done on the second night as well, and one studies at the table on both nights a Mishnah from Tractate Rosh Hashanah (with a pleasant melody, with intent toward the Name Adonai), and it is customary to study also the language of the Zohar printed in the Machzorim.
takeaways: One blesses "Shehecheyanu" on both nights; on the second night a new fruit is good (but not essential)
One studies a Mishnah from Tractate Rosh Hashanah and the language of the Zohar on both nights

paragraphs: If the night of the mitzvah immersion falls on the night of Rosh Hashanah, he should have marital relations and immerse in the morning; and one who piously wishes to postpone marital relations connected with the mitzvah immersion, this is a foolish piety. And even if it is not a mitzvah immersion, if he sees that his desire for his wife has become greatly aroused, he should have relations and immerse in the morning, so that he not come, God forbid, to the impurity of seminal emission; and every person knows himself.

clarification.explanation: If the night of the mitzvah immersion (the wife's night of immersion) falls on the night of Rosh Hashanah, he should have relations and immerse in the morning, and one who is stringent to postpone relations connected with the mitzvah immersion - this is a foolish piety. And even if it is not a mitzvah immersion, if he sees that his desire has become greatly aroused, he should have relations and immerse in the morning, so as not to come to the impurity of seminal emission; and every person knows himself.
takeaways: A mitzvah immersion falling on the night of Rosh Hashanah: he has relations and immerses in the morning; postponing this is a foolish piety
If his desire is greatly aroused, he should have relations to prevent seminal emission

paragraphs: The two days of Rosh Hashanah have one [continuous] holiness, and an egg laid on the first day is forbidden on the second, and likewise something trapped or plucked on the first day is forbidden on the second. And if Rosh Hashanah falls on Thursday and Friday, it is forbidden also on the Shabbat that follows them; and if it is doubtful whether something came into being on Erev Rosh Hashanah or on the day of Rosh Hashanah itself, it is forbidden.

clarification.explanation: The two days of Rosh Hashanah have one continuous holiness, and therefore an egg laid on the first day is forbidden also on the second, and likewise something trapped or plucked on this day is forbidden on the second day. And if Rosh Hashanah falls on Thursday and Friday, the prohibition continues also to the Shabbat that follows them. And if it is doubtful whether the thing came into being on Erev Rosh Hashanah or on Rosh Hashanah itself, it is forbidden.
takeaways: The two days of Rosh Hashanah are one continuous holiness: what is born or trapped on one day is forbidden on the other
If they fall on Thursday and Friday, the egg is forbidden even on the following Shabbat; a doubtful case is forbidden

paragraphs: One does not sleep during the day on Rosh Hashanah, and one must be careful to wake from his sleep at night before dawn. And if he has a headache or some other ailment that forces him to sleep during the day, he should restrain himself and sleep only after midday.

clarification.explanation: One does not sleep during the daytime of Rosh Hashanah, and one must take care to wake up at night before dawn. And one who has a headache or another ailment that forces him to sleep during the day should restrain himself and sleep only after midday.
takeaways: One does not sleep during the day on Rosh Hashanah, and one wakes before dawn
One who must sleep because of an ailment should wait until after midday

paragraphs: The order of Tashlich is performed even if Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat, and so it is found written in the handwriting of Rabbi Yehuda Antebi, of blessed memory, in the name of our teacher the Rashash, of blessed memory. And if one was prevented and did not perform Tashlich on the first day, he should perform it on the second day after Musaf; so I found written in the book Torah LiShmah, in manuscript.

clarification.explanation: One performs the order of Tashlich even when Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat, as Rabbi Yehuda Antebi wrote in the name of the Rashash. And one who was prevented and did not perform Tashlich on the first day should perform it on the second day after the Musaf prayer, as [the Ben Ish Chai] found written in the book Torah LiShmah.
takeaways: Tashlich is performed even on Shabbat
One who was prevented and did not perform it on the first day performs it on the second day after Musaf

paragraphs: On Rosh Hashanah one does not say "Pardon and forgive our sins," and one must be careful in the supplication recited before and after the Psalms [Tehillim] to skip these expressions. And although the Holy Zohar writes that it is forbidden to specify one's sins on this day, this refers specifically to doing so aloud; but in a whisper, at the time of the "Meyushav" shofar blowing, when the blower pauses between Tashrat and Tashat, and between Tashat and Tarat, one may confess his sins in detail in a whisper, and in the Siddur of our teacher the Rashash, of blessed memory, a text of confession is arranged to be recited between these sets.

clarification.explanation: On Rosh Hashanah one does not say "Pardon and forgive our sins," and one must be careful to skip these expressions in the supplications recited before and after Tehillim. And although the Zohar writes that it is forbidden to specify one's sins on this day, this means specifically aloud; but in a whisper, during the "Meyushav" [seated] shofar blowings, when the blower pauses between the sets of blasts (Tashrat, Tashat, Tarat), one may confess his sins in detail in a whisper, and in the Siddur of the Rashash a text of confession is arranged for between the sets.
takeaways: One does not say "Pardon and forgive" on Rosh Hashanah; these expressions are skipped
It is permitted to confess in a whisper (not aloud) between the sets of the seated shofar blowings

paragraphs: He should say explicitly before he blows: "I am hereby prepared, with these blowings, both of the seated [blowing] and of the standing [blowing], to fulfill the obligation of all who hear, in all of them." Even though he is presumably already prepared for this, it is good to state it explicitly with his mouth. Neither the blower nor the congregation should converse between the blowings of the "seated" set and the blowings of the "standing" set. And the verses and the liturgical poem that the congregation is accustomed to recite before the Musaf prayer, after the return of the Torah scroll to the ark, should not be recited by the blower.

clarification.explanation: Before the blowings he should state explicitly: "I am hereby prepared, with these blowings, both of the seated and of the standing [sets], to fulfill the obligation of all who hear" - even though he is presumably prepared for this anyway, it is good to state it explicitly. The blower and the congregation should not converse between the blowings of the "seated" set and those of the "standing" set. The verses and the liturgical poem that the congregation customarily recites before Musaf (after the return of the Torah scroll) should not be recited by the blower.
takeaways: The blower declares aloud that he intends to fulfill the obligation for the listeners
One does not converse between the seated and standing blowings; the blower does not recite the poem before Musaf

paragraphs: He should keep the shofar covered until the blessings are finished, and he must hold it in his hand covered at the time of the blessing - see Rosh Mashbir, siman 30. Before the blessing he should strike his hand on the bimah so that the whole congregation will sense that he is ready to bless and will pay attention to the blessing, and he should say "By the permission of my teachers and masters," and bless aloud, intending to fulfill the obligation for the congregation. And if there is a person sitting far from the blower whose hearing is weak, so that he certainly does not hear the blessings well, he should bless for himself when the blower blesses, and [then] listen to the blowings. In some places it is customary to stand during the blessing of the shofar blowing, and in some places it is not customary to stand; and in our city it was not customary to stand.

clarification.explanation: The blower keeps the shofar covered until the blessings are finished, and holds it in his hand covered during the blessing (see Rosh Mashbir). Before the blessing he strikes his hand on the bimah, so that the whole congregation will sense that he is ready to bless and pay attention, and he says "By the permission of my teachers and masters," and blesses aloud, intending to fulfill the obligation for the congregation. And if there is a person sitting far from the blower whose hearing is weak, so that he certainly does not hear the blessings well, he should bless for himself while the blower blesses, and listen to the blowings. In some places it is customary to stand at the blessing of the shofar blowing, and in some it is not; and in our city it was not customary to stand.
takeaways: The blower holds the shofar covered during the blessing, strikes the bimah so people will pay attention, says "By the permission of my teachers and masters," and blesses aloud to fulfill the obligation for the congregation.
One who sits far away with weak hearing should bless for himself and [then] listen to the blowings.
Some are accustomed to stand at the blessing and some are not (and in his city they did not stand).

paragraphs: He should hold the shofar in his right hand and position it also on the right side, if possible; and for the first blowing too, the one who calls out [the sequence] should call it out to him. And he must be careful that the shofar not be blemished at all at the place where the mouth is placed, even the slightest blemish, and it should be fixed before Rosh Hashanah.

clarification.explanation: He should hold the shofar in his right hand and position it to the right side if possible, and even for the first blowing the caller should call out [the sequence] to him. He must be careful that the shofar not be blemished at all at the place where the mouth is placed, even a slight blemish, and it should be fixed before Rosh Hashanah.
takeaways: He holds the shofar in his right hand and to the right side; even for the first blowing the caller calls out the sequence to him
The shofar must not be blemished at the place where the mouth is placed; it is fixed before Rosh Hashanah

paragraphs: One who was prevented and did not come to the synagogue, and the blower comes to his home to blow for him three times Tashrat, three times Tashat, and three times Tarat, must stand during the blowings, since for him these constitute an obligation from the Torah, and he must be standing, similar to the counting of the Omer, because he does not hear the blowings in the order of the Musaf prayer, and through these he fulfills his Biblical obligation. Women are exempt from this law, since this is a positive, time-bound commandment; but most women have accepted this mitzvah upon themselves as an obligation and come to the synagogue to hear the sound of the shofar, and therefore a woman who has been accustomed to do so for several years, it becomes for her an obligation by acceptance. And if she was prevented and could not come to the synagogue, the blower should come to her house and blow for her, but she should not recite the blessing; and so we were accustomed in our home. And a woman who was accustomed in this mitzvah and it happened once that she could not come to the synagogue and also could not bring a blower to her house, she should perform, on Erev Rosh Hashanah, an annulment (hatarah) of her acceptance of the custom.

clarification.explanation: One who was prevented and did not come to the synagogue, and the blower comes to his home to blow for him three times Tashrat, three Tashat, and three Tarat, must stand during the blowings, since for him these constitute a Biblical obligation (like the counting of the Omer), because he does not hear the blowings in the order of Musaf, and through these he fulfills his Biblical obligation. Women are exempt from this obligation (a positive, time-bound commandment), but most women have accepted this mitzvah upon themselves as an obligation and come to hear the shofar, and therefore a woman who has been accustomed to do so for several years, it becomes an obligation for her; and if she was prevented, the blower should come to her home and blow for her without a blessing. And if she cannot even bring a blower, she should perform, on Erev Rosh Hashanah, an annulment of her acceptance of the custom.
takeaways: One who is prevented and hears the blowings at home stands, since for him they are a Biblical obligation
A woman who has been accustomed to the mitzvah becomes obligated in it; if prevented, she hears it at home without a blessing, or performs an annulment

paragraphs: From Rosh Hashanah until Yom Kippur one says "HaMelech HaKadosh" [the Holy King], and if one said "HaEl HaKadosh" [the Holy God] or is in doubt, he returns to the beginning of the prayer. And if he said "HaEl HaKadosh" and immediately remembered and concluded "HaMelech HaKadosh," so that his recitation was "HaEl HaKadosh HaMelech HaKadosh," he has fulfilled his obligation. And if the prayer leader erred in the repetition, he too returns to the beginning and repeats the Kedushah. And likewise the same law applies to the blessing "Me'ein Sheva" [the abbreviated Friday-night blessing]; and although there are those who differ regarding the blessing "Me'ein Sheva," we do not say "when in doubt about blessings, be lenient" against the opinion of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, who held that the blessing "Me'ein Sheva" stands in place of the repetition, as I have written in my holy book Makabtziel.

clarification.explanation: From Rosh Hashanah until Yom Kippur one says "HaMelech HaKadosh." If one said "HaEl HaKadosh," or is in doubt, he returns to the beginning of the prayer. And if he said "HaEl HaKadosh" and immediately remembered and concluded "HaMelech HaKadosh" (so that he said "HaEl HaKadosh HaMelech HaKadosh") he has fulfilled his obligation. Likewise, if the cantor erred in the repetition he returns to the beginning and recites the Kedushah again, and the same applies to the blessing "Me'ein Sheva" (of Friday night). And although there are those who differ regarding "Me'ein Sheva," one does not say "when in doubt about blessings, be lenient" against the opinion of the Ari, that this blessing stands in place of the repetition.
takeaways: During the Ten Days of Repentance: "HaMelech HaKadosh"; one who erred or is in doubt returns to the beginning of the prayer
One who corrected himself immediately after "HaEl HaKadosh" has fulfilled his obligation; a cantor who erred returns and repeats the Kedushah

paragraphs: In the blessing "Hashivah" [Restore our judges] one says "HaMelech HaMishpat" [the King of judgment]. And if he erred and said "Melech Ohev Tzedakah U'Mishpat" [King who loves righteousness and judgment], since he mentioned "Melech" [King], he does not return - and although Maran, of blessed memory, holds that he should return, we follow "when in doubt about blessings, be lenient," even against the opinion of Maran, of blessed memory, as I have written in my holy book Makabtziel.

clarification.explanation: In the blessing "Hashivah Shofteinu" [Restore our judges], one says, during the Ten Days of Repentance, "HaMelech HaMishpat." And if he erred and said "Melech Ohev Tzedakah U'Mishpat," since he mentioned "Melech," he does not return. And although Maran holds that he should return, we follow "when in doubt about blessings, be lenient," even against his opinion.
takeaways: In the blessing "Hashivah": "HaMelech HaMishpat"
If he erred and said "Melech Ohev Tzedakah U'Mishpat," he does not return, since he mentioned "Melech"

paragraphs: If he concluded the blessing and did not say "Zochreinu" and "Mi Chamocha," he does not return, and even if he said "Baruch Atah Hashem" and then remembered, he is not permitted to conclude "Lamdeni Chukecha" [in order to insert them] so as to say "Zochreinu" and "Mi Chamocha." And it is stated in the book Torah LiShmah that since "Zochreinu" is a request for mercy, if he did not say it in its place he should say it in [the blessing] "Shome'a Tefillah," and on Shabbat and Rosh Hashanah he should say it before he withdraws his feet [at the end of the Amidah]. This is unlike "Mi Chamocha," which has no makeup, since it is not a request for mercy. And likewise regarding the recitation of "V'chetov" [and inscribe] etc. and "U'vesefer" [and in the book] etc., if he forgot, he does not return, but he should say it before he withdraws his feet, since these are requests for mercy.

clarification.explanation: If he concluded the blessing without saying "Zochreinu" or "Mi Chamocha," he does not return, and even if he said "Baruch Atah Hashem" and then remembered, he may not conclude "Lamdeni Chukecha" [instead] in order to say them. According to Torah LiShmah, "Zochreinu," being a request for mercy, if forgotten in its place, should be said in "Shome'a Tefillah" (and on Shabbat and Rosh Hashanah, before withdrawing his feet [at the end of the Amidah]); but "Mi Chamocha" has no makeup, since it is not a request for mercy. Likewise "V'chetov" and "U'vesefer," if forgotten, he does not return, but should say them before withdrawing his feet, since they are requests for mercy.
takeaways: One who forgot "Zochreinu"/"Mi Chamocha" and concluded the blessing does not return
"Zochreinu," "V'chetov," and "U'vesefer" (requests for mercy) can be made up; "Mi Chamocha" cannot

paragraphs: In the Musaf of Rosh Hashanah, of Shabbat Shuvah, and of Yom Kippur, one says "Mi Chamocha Av HaRachamim" [Who is like You, Father of Mercy], and the same law applies at Minchah of Shabbat Shuvah; and even if Rosh Hashanah or Yom Kippur fall on Shabbat, one says at Minchah "Av HaRachamim." And when he says in the Musaf of Rosh Hashanah the verse "Hashem Tzeva'ot yagen aleihem" [Hashem of Hosts shields them], he should make the cantillation of the end of a verse, since this is a verse in Zechariah and this is its ending; but what he says afterward, "Hashem Tzeva'ot yagen aleichem" [shields you], is a request. And when he says "V'atem hadeveikim" etc., when he reaches the letter tav of "tichtevenu" [may You inscribe us], he should skip the word "hayom" [today], since one should not consider oneself a completely righteous person who is inscribed on Rosh Hashanah [itself], as mentioned in the Levush; and he should be careful to say "tichtevenu berachamecha lechayim tovim" [may You inscribe us in Your mercy for a good life] for the sake of the acrostic, that it not spell out 439. And likewise at the letter peh he should say "hayom tifkedeinu berachamecha lechayim tovim" [today may You recall us in Your mercy for a good life].

clarification.explanation: In the Musaf of Rosh Hashanah, Shabbat Shuvah, and Yom Kippur one says "Mi Chamocha Av HaRachamim," and likewise at Minchah of Shabbat Shuvah, and even if Rosh Hashanah or Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat, one says "Av HaRachamim" at Minchah. In the Musaf of Rosh Hashanah, when saying "Hashem Tzeva'ot yagen aleihem," one uses the cantillation for the end of a verse (since this is a verse in Zechariah), but the following "Hashem Tzeva'ot yagen aleichem" is a request. And in "V'atem hadeveikim," upon reaching the letter tav of "tichtevenu," one skips the word "hayom" [today], so as not to consider oneself a completely righteous person immediately inscribed on Rosh Hashanah, and says "tichtevenu berachamecha lechayim tovim" (for the sake of the acrostic); and at the letter peh, one says "hayom tifkedeinu berachamecha lechayim tovim" - specifically including the word "today," unlike at the letter tav.
takeaways: One says "Mi Chamocha Av HaRachamim" at Musaf and at Shabbat Shuvah

In "V'atem hadeveikim": at the letter tav one skips "today" and says "tichtevenu berachamecha lechayim tovim"; at the letter peh one says "hayom tifkedeinu berachamecha lechayim tovim" - with the word "today"

paragraphs: When he says "Zochreinu LeChayim" [Remember us for life], he should intend to draw down life for the soul; and when he says "Kotveinu BeSefer Chayim" [Inscribe us in the book of life], he should intend to draw down life for the body. And he should intend the beginning of "Zochreinu" as the letter zayin (numerical value 7) and its end as the letter mem (numerical value 40), the number of the Names Havayah and Ehyeh, which are Chochmah and Binah. And when he says "Zocher Yetzurav BeRachamim LeChayim" [Who remembers His creatures in mercy, for life], he should intend this regarding the souls that He remembers in His mercy to bring them back to life, to give them life in this world, in the secret of their return through reincarnation, and from this the matter of the resurrection of the dead is confirmed for us. And when he says "HaYom Harat Olam, im keVanim im ka'Avadim" [Today is the birth of the world; whether as sons or as servants], our teacher the Rashash, of blessed memory, wrote that when one says this, all his bones should seize him with trembling, as if to say: "If I am a father, where is My honor, and if I am a master, where is My awe" [that He may recall it]. Therefore he should say this slowly and with a broken heart; and therefore the custom is that this too is said in the repetition, aloud, by the congregation, in addition to the prayer leader.

clarification.explanation: Among the intentions in the prayer: when saying "Zochreinu LeChayim," one intends to draw life to the soul, and when saying "Kotveinu BeSefer Chayim," to draw life to the body. "Zocher Yetzurav BeRachamim LeChayim" is directed at the souls that Hashem returns to life in the secret of reincarnation, from which the matter of the resurrection of the dead is confirmed for us. "HaYom Harat Olam, im keVanim im ka'Avadim" should be said slowly and with a broken heart, so that all one's bones tremble as he says: if as sons, where is His honor, and if as servants, where is His awe; and therefore the custom is to say it also in the repetition, aloud, by the congregation (in addition to the cantor).
takeaways: The intentions of "Zochreinu"/"Kotveinu": life for the soul and for the body; "Zocher Yetzurav" alludes to the resurrection of the dead
"HaYom Harat Olam" is said slowly and with a broken heart, also in the repetition, aloud

paragraphs: In the text of the "Yehi Ratzon" after Tehillim it is written "that we merit and live seventy years, and if with strength, eighty years" - but how can an old man whose years already exceed eighty say this? And furthermore, even one who has not yet reached seventy - why should he ask for a fixed measure, when perhaps Hashem will grant him more years? Therefore he should not say this text, but should say instead: "that we merit long, good, and proper years" - and in this text there is certainly a secret, for it is the text with which the High Priest is blessed at the conclusion of Yom Kippur, as he emerges in peace from the Holy [place].

clarification.explanation: In the text of the "Yehi Ratzon" recited after Tehillim it is written "that we merit and live seventy years, and if with strength, eighty years" - but how can an elderly person who has already passed eighty say this? And furthermore, why should a person ask for a fixed measure, when perhaps Hashem will give him more? Therefore one should not say this text, but should say "that we merit long, good, and proper years," and this text contains a secret, for with it the High Priest is blessed at the conclusion of Yom Kippur as he emerges in peace from the Holy place.
takeaways: One does not say "seventy years... eighty years" (a fixed number)
One says "that we merit long, good, and proper years"

paragraphs: During the Ten Days of Repentance one does not undertake a "hafsakah" fast [one that continues into the night], for it is not proper to fast also at night during these days, since in these days the essential rectification is achieved through eating and drinking; and were we not compelled to fast during the day for the rectification of our sins, we would not fast even during the day. Now that we do fast during the day, we rely on completing the rectification through the eating and drinking of the night. Therefore it is written in the book Torah LiShmah that one should eat bread every night during the Ten Days of Repentance, in order to recite Birkat HaMazon [Grace after Meals].

clarification.explanation: During the Ten Days of Repentance one does not observe a "hafsakah" fast (one continuing into the night), since it is not proper to fast at night during these days, because in these days the essential rectification is achieved specifically through eating and drinking; and were we not compelled to fast during the day for the rectification of our sins, we would not fast at all, and therefore we complete the rectification through the eating and drinking of the night. Therefore Torah LiShmah writes that one should eat bread every night during the Ten Days of Repentance in order to recite Birkat HaMazon.
takeaways: One does not fast at night during the Ten Days of Repentance, since the rectification is achieved through eating and drinking
One eats bread every night in order to recite Birkat HaMazon

paragraphs: A young married woman [kallah] who, together with her husband, relies on the table of her father-in-law and mother-in-law - and so throughout the year her mother-in-law separates challah from the dough and blesses [over it] - during the Ten Days of Repentance she should make an effort to take money from her husband and purchase with it flour in the measure of challah, so that she herself may fulfill the mitzvah of separating challah with a blessing, at least once a year.

clarification.explanation: A young married woman who, along with her husband, relies on the table of her father-in-law and mother-in-law - and throughout the year the mother-in-law separates challah and blesses - during the Ten Days of Repentance should make an effort to take money from her husband and buy with it flour in the measure of challah, so that she herself may fulfill the mitzvah of separating challah with a blessing, at least once a year.
takeaways: A young wife who relies on her mother-in-law's table should separate challah herself during the Ten Days of Repentance
In order to fulfill the mitzvah with a blessing at least once a year
